title: Construction Management Research Methods
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to cultivate a comprehensive understanding of research within the field of construction management. Students will be exposed to the fundamental nature of research and the processes involved in its execution. The course will explore the contemporary structure of research and familiarise students with various research methodologies, including quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-mode approaches. This course will guide students in utilising online resources and tools for efficient searching, identification, and retrieval of relevant research materials. This course also aims at introducing common data analysis techniques, enabling students to effectively process and interpret research findings. A critical component of the course focuses on fostering effective communication skills for research outcomes within the context of construction management. Students will be equipped to translate complex findings into impactful presentations and written reports specifically tailored for this audience. This course aligns with the program's intent to develop and apply research, communication, and professional skills.
learning_outcomes: Develop a comprehensive understanding of research fundamentals.
Develop an understanding of quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-mode research methodologies relevant to construction management.
Develop an understanding of appropriate data analysis techniques to interpret and draw meaningful conclusions from research findings.
Develop proficient communication skills to articulate research outcomes clearly and effectively
Develop skills in utilising online resources and tools proficiently to search, identify, retrieve, and critically evaluate relevant research materials
Develop a thorough understanding of key ethical considerations in research
incompatibilities: Must not have completed CONMGNT_7008 Construction Research Methods at the University of Adelaide

title: Geotechnical Engineering Design
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: The aim of this course is to master the application and extension of soil mechanics principles to design of common geotechnical structures such as retaining walls, shallow and deep foundation, stable slopes along with mastery of concepts and approaches related to site Investigation, earth pressure calculation and sustainability in construction practices.
learning_outcomes: Understand the principles and techniques of site investigation, including soil sampling, drilling, and geophysical surveys, to effectively develop an idealised geotechnical model for design

Analyse earth pressures and apply relevant theories to determine lateral forces acting on retaining structures, enabling the design of stable and structurally sound nonembedded and embedded retaining walls
Evaluate shallow foundation design considerations, such as soil reactivity and bearing capacity, to design footings that safely distribute structural loads and minimise settlement
Explore deep foundation systems, including piles and drilled shafts, and apply design principles to ensure adequate load-bearing capacity and settlement control in diverse soil conditions

Identify slope instability mechanisms, assess slope stability using analytical and numerical methods, and implement appropriate mitigation measures to ensure the stability and safety of engineered slopes in various geological environments
Sustainability in construction practice and use of recycled materials in geotechnical construction
prerequisites: Must have completedENGM2010Soil Mechanics
incompatibilities: Must not have completed CIVE3007 Geotechnical Engineering at University of South Australia AND must not have completed CIVILENG 3006 Geothecnical Engineering at University of Adelaide

title: Honours Biomedicine Research Project Part 2
school: School of Pharm and Biomed Sci
syllabus_overview: This course forms the main basis of an honours project conducted in the School of Biomedicine. Students will be expected to engage in a novel, independent research project under the guidance of a principal supervisor and co-supervisor(s) focussed on key research areas in Anatomy, Pathology, Pharmacology, Physiology, or Reproduction and Development. To complete the course, students will be required to prepare and deliver a project proposal and resource pro-forma. This course provides an advanced insight into the scientific research process and develops professional attributes and skills.
learning_outcomes: Execute a well-defined research project, under the guidance of a project supervisor
Critically interpret the background literature relevant to the research project.

Demonstrate mastery of the techniques required for the experimental study of a research question,including collection, storage, and evaluation of data which is rigorous and methodical in accordancewith the Australian Code for Responsible Practice of Research.
Identify and evaluate methodological or technical issues in a research project and define the importantelements required to solve them.
Communicate the elements of the research project clearly and concisely in spoken and written English.
prerequisites: Must have completed HLTH1035 Honours Biomedicine Research Project Part 1 OR must have completed HLTH4022 Honours Biomedicine Research Project Part 1
incompatibilities: Must not have completed all of HLTH1036 Honours Biomedicine Research Project Part 2/HLTHSC4510B Honours Biomedicine Research Project Part 2 at the University of Adelaide

title: Intellectual Property Law
syllabus_overview: This course provides an overview of the different regimes of Intellectual Property law including trademarks, copyright, design, and patents, with a focus on how these laws can be adapted and utilised to promote social, global, and climate justice. The course will provide students with the knowledge and skills they need to advise clients about the legal options available to protect creative effort. Students will consider how Intellectual Property laws attempt to balance competing public and private interests such as the encouragement of innovation versus the encouragement of knowledge transfer and competition. Students will critically analyse how Intellectual Property laws can be leveraged to support the development and dissemination of technologies and creative works that contribute to social equity, global health, and environmental sustainability. They will also examine how these laws can be reformed to better serve marginalised communities, promote access to essential resources and technologies, and encourage the creation of sustainable and socially responsible innovations. By researching the different Intellectual Property regimes, students will be equipped to determine how they can be used to protect hypothetical creative effort. They will undertake searches of Intellectual Property databases and draft applications and legal documents to obtain appropriate protection. By the end of the course, students will be equipped with a comprehensive understanding of Intellectual Property law and its potential to drive positive social change, as well as the practical skills needed to advise clients and shape the future of this dynamic field in a manner that promotes justice and sustainability.
learning_outcomes: Compare the Intellectual Property regimes and identify and explain the elements that are relevant to each one

Conduct research of Intellectual Property regimes, including legislation and cases, to determine which regimes apply to a hypothetical creative effort and explain their application and relevant issues
Conduct searches on relevant Intellectual Property databases to determine the merits of obtaining protection for a hypothetical creative effort
Draft relevant applications and other required documents to apply for protection of a hypothetical creative effort addressing each of the elements of the relevant Intellectual Property regimes

title: Renewable Energy Systems
school: School of Elec and Mech Eng
syllabus_overview: The aim of this course is to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of renewable energy systems, with a primary focus on solar photovoltaic and wind energy technologies, their underlying physical principles, electrical integration, system modelling, and practical design considerations. The course equips students with the ability to analyse renewable energy resources, model and evaluate PV and wind energy systems, assess their technical, economic, and environmental performance, and design grid-connected, off-grid, and microgrid-based solutions incorporating energy storage. Through an Australian and global context, the course prepares students to understand the role of renewable energy in modern power systems and to apply fundamental engineering concepts to real-world renewable energy applications.
learning_outcomes: Define and describe renewable energy concepts such as: solar/wind power conversion, maximum power point tracking, generation-duration curve, capacity factor, grid-connected inverters, islanding, levelized cost of energy
Describe the functions of the key components of solar and wind power generation systems and battery energy storage systems
Analyse the performance of a given solar generation system
Analyse the performance of a given wind generation system
Design a battery storage system to meet a given requirement
Integrate renewable energy systems at a system level
incompatibilities: Must not have completed EEET 3050 at University of South Australia AND must not have completed ENG 4062 at University of Adelaide

assessment_tasks.task_name: Problem Solving Task, Problem Solving Task
Problem Solving Task, Problem Solving Task

title: Steel Concrete Composite Design
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: This course equips students with skills to design steel concrete composites including the design of composite slabs, beams and columns, the design of shear connectors based on the concepts of shear connection and interaction.
learning_outcomes: Describe the principles of steel concrete composite design, including the impact of differing degrees of shear connection and shear interaction
Analyse, design and detail composite slabs and beams subjected to flexure and shear according to AS/NZS 2327
Analyse, design and detail composite columns subjected to combined axial, bending and shear according to AS/NZS 2327
Design and detail composite slabs and beams to allow for the introduction of openings and service ducts according to AS/NZS 2327
prerequisites: Must have completedENGCX302Reinforced Concrete Design AND must have completedENGCX304Structural Steel Design

assessment_tasks.task_name: Problem Solving Task, Problem Solving Task, Problem Solving Task, Problem Solving Task, Problem Solving Task

title: Construction Planning and Safety
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: This course aims to equip students with foundational knowledge and practical skills in construction scheduling, enabling them to plan, organise, and control project timelines using both deterministic and stochastic methods. Students will develop the ability to analyse activities, allocate resources effectively, and anticipate potential delays to enhance efficiency and minimise risks in construction projects. This course further develops students’ understanding of construction safety legislation, risk management, and industry standards. This course enables students to assess hazards, investigate accidents, and apply effective control measures, while developing skills to promote ethical and legal responsibilities that prioritise worker wellbeing. Through applying safety alongside construction planning principles, students will be ready to manage projects confidently and responsibly in the dynamic construction industry.
learning_outcomes: Explain the principles of time management and their application in planning and scheduling construction projects.
Apply deterministic and stochastic scheduling techniques to develop, analyse, and control construction project timelines.
Analyse construction site hazards and causes of accidents.
Evaluate risk management strategies for construction sites to ensure compliance with WHS regulations and industry standards
Integrate safety management systems and practices into the preparation of safe work method statements
prerequisites: must have completed BLDG1000 Introduction to Construction Management

title: Numerical Methods in Geotechnical Design
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: The aim of this course focus on the utilisation of cutting-edge engineering software packages to tackle sophisticated engineering challenges. Topics will encompass solving partial differential equations in solid mechanics and finite difference. The course will mainly emphasise employing numerical and computational methods, including discrete elements, finite difference and finite elements. Students will also explore commercial engineering packages, with a keen focus on establishing accuracy standards. Through this, participants will gain proficiency in applying advanced computational techniques to address complex engineering problems effectively.
learning_outcomes: Understand the principles of particle morphology, solid mechanics and continuum mechanics
Demonstrate proficiency in analytical methods and computational techniques for modelling particle morphology and simulating particle interactions
Demonstrate problem-solving skills by applying analytical and computational approaches to address challenges related to solid mechanics in engineering practice
Develop proficiency in discretising complex geotechnical problems solving linear and nonlinear equations in both static and dynamic problems

Develop DEM and FEM simulations using specialised software tools tailored for geotechnical engineering applications and evaluate the simulation results, and gain hands-on experience through these exercises

title: Water Engineering Hydraulics and Modelling
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: This course delves into advanced topics of hydraulic systems for civil engineers. Students will explore both the fundamental theories and the practical skills necessary for designing and managing pipeline and open channel systems. The curriculum includes in-depth modules on pipeline systems, covering minor loss elements, pumps, pipe networks, and extended period simulations. For open channel systems, the course will cover flow profile plotting and computation, 1D flow profile simulation, and hydraulics structures such as weirs, spillways, sluice gates, and channel networks. Additionally, students will engage in laboratory practicals and undertake a comprehensive design project to apply their theoretical knowledge in real-world scenarios.
learning_outcomes: Identify the relevant theoretical frameworks for problems relating to pipeline and open channel systems
Develop and execute solution strategies for problems relating to pipeline and open channel systems
Develop and apply computer modelling techniques to pipeline and open channel systems
Critically evaluate and effectively synthesise simulation results for pipeline and open channel systems models
Undertake laboratory experiments on a range of hydraulic systems, and employ appropriate hydraulics theory to analyse measured data
Apply pipeline and open channel system design principles to a semi-structured design problem and write a comprehensive technical design report
incompatibilities: Must not have completed CIVE3010 AND must not have completed CIVE3009 AND must not have completed CIVENG 3005

assessment_tasks.task_name: Data Collection and/or Analysis, Data Collection and/or Analysis, Data Collection and/or Analysis

title: Economics of International Trade
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with an in-depth understanding of the theories, policies, and economic impacts of international trade. It provides students with a thorough grounding in the theory of international trade as well as international trade policy. It demonstrates the relevance of the theory in the analysis of (a) existing patterns of international trade and what determines them, (b) the conduct of trade policy and (c) the economic implications of international trade and trade policy both for individual economies such as Australia and the wider international community.
learning_outcomes: Compare the major models of international trade and distinguish between them in terms of their assumptions and economic implications.
Analyse the economic effects of trade policy instruments, retaliatory measures, and the formation of regional trading arrangements.
Distinguish and critically analyse the main arguments for protection and critically evaluate the relevance and realism of arguments for free trade.
Identify major recent developments in the world trading system and critically analyse key issues raised by both multilateral trade agreements and the spread of regional trading arrangements.

Analyse the relationship between international trade theory and trade flows through evidence-based analysis, and evaluate how interactions among trade policy, trade practice, and geopolitics can lead to sub-optimal welfare and growth outcomes.
prerequisites: must have completed 1 of ECON2002 Intermediate Applied Econometrics/ECON2006 Intermediate Econometrics AND must have completed 1 of ECON2003 Intermediate Applied Microeconomics/ECON2005 Intermediate Microeconomics

title: Business Process Management
syllabus_overview: The course aims to equip learners with skills to manage organisational transformation effectively through systematic approaches to workflow modelling and management of business processes. The course builds upon business process management and strategy theory in order to analyse business processes. The learners will learn how to identify business process improvements and opportunities for business process reengineering, automation and digital business transformation. By examining business processes, learners will work individually and in teams to gain insight into the role of a business analyst in the agile organisational environment. This course aligns with the program intent to provide a comprehensive understanding of business process modelling in the context of enterprise IT management.
learning_outcomes: Develop business strategies and models to frame organisational transformation with consideration of IT infrastructure
Demonstrate the principles of business process management
Analyse the internal and external forces driving and influencing organisational transformation
Analyse the legal, cultural and ethical implications of operating a business in a global environment
Apply business process modelling techniques within a specific organisational context
Apply business process management techniques to realise organisational objectives

assessment_tasks.task_name: A range of assignments designed to support course outcomes

title: Animal Management 3
school: School of Animal and Vet Sci
syllabus_overview: Animal management is provided by local and State/Territory governments to protect the safety and comfort of communities by administering domestic animal legislation, and through community education and engagement. Companion animals are an important part of people's lives, and managing them appropriately maximises the benefits of animal companionship for all of society. This course will provide knowledge and skills necessary for the management of animals, in particular dogs and cats but including livestock and wildlife species. Such skills are relevant for work in local government, or animal shelters or animal welfare organisations. Topics will include interpreting body language, assessing risk when handling individual animals and selecting appropriate equipment, using an evidence based approach to evaluate and design initiatives to resolve community problems caused by animals (e.g. dog attacks, dog barking, cat management), community engagement and conflict management. The course will include a week of online learning followed by a week of face to face workshops and practical classes.
learning_outcomes: Observe and interpret behavioural signs of emotional states (e.g. stress) in dogs and cats and apply safe handling practices to aggressive or anxious dogs and cats and other relevant species (e.g. wildlife)

Describe approaches to dealing with barking dogs, and other conflicts that may occur due to interactions between animals and people in local government areas and outline the basis of conflict resolution
Discuss complex areas of animal management (e.g. dog attacks and cat management) and evidence based approaches in these areas
Explore a range of strategies to increase community engagement and effect behaviour change relevant to animal management in the community
Outline the regulation of dogs and cats in Australia, and the importance of ethical and societal considerations in management plans

title: Environmental Technologies 3
school: School of Phys, Chem and E Sci
syllabus_overview: The aim of this course is to provide students with an in-depth understanding of the various technologies available for the prevention, treatment and remediation of environmental issues in air, soil and water systems. The course will cover technologies and approaches related to carbon capture, storage and sequestration, contaminated land remediation, mine site rehabilitation, treatment and recycling of nutrient from waste streams. Students will learn about existing and emerging technologies and assess whether they provide solutions with meaningful results for the environment.
learning_outcomes: Outline and discuss the theoretical basis for a range of technological solutions aimed at mitigating and repairing societal influences on the carbon cycle
Undertake basic calculations to assess the impact, practical applicability and/or validity of various environmental technologies
Integrate existing scientific knowledge, information and datasets to outline solutions to environmental quality problems at a given site/locality
Work as part of a team to research and assess technology solutions
Provide recommendations for the implementation of technology solutions and/or outline considerations for government policy development
Communicate scientific findings in a professional manner
prerequisites: Must have completed CHEM1004 Introduction to Environmental Chemistry OR must have completedAGRI2004Soil and Water Resources 2 OR must have completedEART2011Geochemistry 2

title: Fine Art Practice and Research
syllabus_overview: Fine Arts Practice and Research reviews key theory and concepts applied in contemporary art practice and practice-based research in the fine arts. It will build upon students’ understanding of practice and research in the field, while introducing advanced methods and methodologies through an examination of case-studies. Students will interrogate their motivations, interests and practices to locate their work within the expansive field of contemporary art and develop a research plan. The course cultivates critical thinking and problem-solving skills, equipping students with skills to engage with pressing contemporary issues and communicate their ideas effectively, whether in professional practice or practice-based research in higher degrees.
learning_outcomes: Articulate relevant concepts applied in contemporary art practice and research methodologies to a level appropriate for professional practice or further research.
Demonstrate understanding of practice and research in the field through discussion of methodologies and methods and analysis of historical and contemporary artists.
Interrogate motivations, interests, and techniques to locate their practice within the broad field of art and creative practice.
Demonstrate critical engagement with contemporary issues in art or society and application of these insights to create a rigorous creative project proposal.
Communicate ideas effectively in writing, in contexts of professional practice and/or creative research practice.

title: Reinforced Concrete Design
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: This course equips students with the fundamentals of sustainable reinforced concrete design including the design of beams and slabs for bending and shear, the design of columns under combined axial bending and shear loads and the basics of detailing of reinforcement.
learning_outcomes: Understand and apply the principles of reinforced concrete design including the impacts of time effects and member cross section on strength, stiffness and ductility
Analyse and design members subjected to the single and combined actions of axial loading, bending and shear
Demonstrate application of AS3600 to the design of reinforced concrete elements
Make decisions informed by an understanding of the environmental impact of reinforced concrete construction and apply this knowledge to the design of concrete structures
prerequisites: Must have completed all of ENGC2001 Introduction to Structural Design - Loads and Forms/ENGM2008 Mechanics of Materials and Structures
incompatibilities: Must not have completed CIVE3003 Reinforced Concrete Design at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed CEME3002 Reinforced Concrete Design at the University of Adelaide

title: Masters Engineering Research Project A
school: School of Elec and Mech Eng
syllabus_overview: This course develops your ability to execute and deliver engineering projects. It is the first in a series of research project courses where students solve authentic engineering problems supported by academic supervisors in small groups. In Part A, students will work to develop a project plan, literature review, and methodology, for an identified engineering project and build their professional practice skills in engineering management alongside oral and written communication. Students continue the same project in Part B. These project courses must be undertaken in consecutive teaching periods and acceptable progress is required to continue to Part B.
learning_outcomes: Formulate an engineering problem scope from a limited brief, drawing on collaboration with an academic advisor, published works and discipline-specific knowledge, that is suitable for the allocated time frame, and can be completed within the available resources
Critically evaluate the state of the field and previous research by accessing, systematically searching, evaluating and referencing relevant and reliable published works
Identify, select and apply appropriate research methodologies to a complex engineering problem

Demonstrate the ability to work effectively and cooperatively as a member of a team to achieve project outcomes, contributing to team leadership as the situation requires, using effective self and/or team management, review and improvement practices
Use and manage information in a professional context and be aware of common document identification, tracking and control procedures
Synthesise and effectively communicate the rationale, progress and outputs of an engineering project through written and oral means to both technical and nontechnical audiences
Critically assess the issues surrounding the conduct of an identified engineering project including, ethical, cultural, safety, social, environmental and economic impacts, as appropriate
prerequisites: Must have completed all of ENGI5003 Professional Engineering Management/ENGI5006 Engineering Data Analytics
incompatibilities: Must not have completed 1 of ENGG 5020 at the University of South Australia/MECHENG7049A at the University of Adelaide

title: Climate Change Adaptation and Resilience
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: The purpose of this course is to consolidate student knowledge on projected climate change impacts and build an in-depth understanding of inclusive, respectful design strategies that can be developed and applied to help adapt to these impacts. The course has a strong focus on concepts of resilience and resilient design principles. Students will consider climate change mitigation and (mal)adaptation, to help guide synergistic solutions contributing to a sustainable future. Students will apply engineering design principles to a range of real-world sectors and settings (such as food systems, housing and built infrastructure and natural ecosystems), in order to develop climate-resilient pathways.
learning_outcomes: Identify and synthesise information required to describe the nature, extent, and uncertainty of projected climate change under different scenarios, in terms of changes to average conditions, extreme events and natural disasters, and how these changes may affect human and non-human systems

Describe what is meant by ‘resilience’ in relation to different human and natural systems, including different disciplinary perspectives / definitions of resilience (Ecology, Disaster Risk, Social Sciences, Infrastructure) and apply these definitions in the context of climate change

Apply the key principles of resilient design to evaluate and critique existing or proposed responses to climate change, in order to identify maladaptive approaches and make synergistic alternative design recommendations

Formulate creative design solutions to improve the resilience of a range of human and natural systems that are vulnerable to future climate change, such as food supply, housing, coastal environments and infrastructure, and natural ecosystems

Communicate topics relating to exposure, vulnerability and resilience in a way that embraces diversity, including inclusive language and clear respect for the knowledge and perspectives of First Nations peoples, and the importance of inclusivity and social justice in adapting to climate change
incompatibilities: Must not have completed UniSA CIVE5074

assessment_tasks.task_name: Peer Review, Peer Review, Peer Review

title: Instrument Flight 1
school: School of Elec and Mech Eng
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will undertake flights conducted under the instrument flight rules (IFR), IFR navigation lessons and 2D and 3D approaches in a simulator and a single engine aircraft. Also: obtain a multi-engine endorsement; instrument flight rule procedures conducted in the simulator, including holding patterns, precision and non precision approaches; multi-engine endorsement training.
learning_outcomes: Be endorsed to operate a multi-engine aircraft in accordance with the pilot operators handbook and CASA Rule Part 61.

Fly a cross country flight under instrument flight rules (IFR), perform holding patterns and approaches utilising the GPS, VOR, ILS and RNAV to the instrument rating standards for issue. Be recommended for progress into Instrument Rating 2.

Demonstrate a professional attitude consistent with an airline pilot applying: good decision making, situational awareness, airmanship and threat and error management by recognising and avoiding potential conflict, deviation from normal operations. Respond correctly to simulated or real in -flight emergencies.

title: Global Population and Health
syllabus_overview: This course aims to introduce students to demographic and geographical perspectives in the study of population health. It provides students with the theoretical foundation, empirical knowledge, and analytical skills to unravel the linkages between the distribution and determinants of health-related states and the environment in populations.
learning_outcomes: Critically explain the major demographic and epidemiological transition models and assess their utility in interpreting how contemporary trends in fertility, mortality, and population ageing shape diverse population health outcomes globally.

Critically analyse the patterns, underlying causes, and multifaceted consequences of pandemics, population mobility, and climate-related health challenges through the integrated lens of demographic and geographical perspectives.

Evaluate the complex interplay of social, housing, environmental, and structural factors in producing and perpetuating health inequalities within and between countries, with a specific focus on the Asia-Pacific region.

Propose and justify evidence-informed policy and intervention options, drawing rigorously upon demographic, geographical, and epidemiological evidence, to mitigate health inequities and enhance population health outcomes.

title: Quantity Surveying Fundamentals and Cost Estimating
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: This course aims to equip learners with fundamental knowledge and skills required for the practice of quantity surveying. The course introduces cost management principles and appropriate knowledge in respect to standard methods of measurement, measurement, bills of quantities, and principles of estimating cost of construction. The learners will develop analytical thinking and effective communication skills for quantity surveying practice. This course intends to introduce learners to the quantity surveying principles enabling them to continue other quantity surveying courses in the program.
learning_outcomes: Describe the role of Quantity Surveyors and cost management principles
Identify how a project scope is broken up into a series of construction trade packages
Demonstrate the ability to read and interpret construction documents
Demonstrate the ability to perform computerised measurement and pricing
Apply principles of standard measurement techniques for construction works
Apply estimating principles for construction works including tender preparation

title: Creative Writing Essentials 3: The Writer as Researcher
syllabus_overview: This course explores approaches to practice-based research in creative writing. Students will conceptualise a research question and plan a structure for a large-scale project. They will be exposed to a range of research methods, as well as the ethical implications of conducting those methods. Students will also learn how to express their research in a range of fiction and creative nonfiction, including prose forms and poetry.
learning_outcomes: Identify a creative project and develop a research plan to complete this project
Demonstrate an understanding of the practicalities of research, including ethics
Create an original piece of publishable writing by drawing on varied and project-appropriate research methods
Evaluate and reflect on research practices and methodologies
Critically read and assess creative and critical writing produced by students themselves, their peers and other writers; offer sensitive feedback to other writers' work

title: Contract Administration
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: This course will provide students with an understanding of: traditional procurement methods and standard forms of contract for construction projects; tendering processes for construction projects; time, payment and variation provisions commonly found in standard forms of construction contracts; and building and construction industry security of payment legislation. Construction Project Lifecycle; Traditional procurement options; Tendering and contract formation; Standard forms of building contracts; Responsibilities of Employer, Contractor and Superintendent in construction contracts.; Nature of contract (bill of quantities and schedule of rates); Practical and final completion of construction contracts.; Progress of construction works and programming; Extensions of time and liquidated damages; Progress payment claims and certificates.; Provisional sums; Set offs; Building and Construction Industry Security of Payment Legislation; Project Bank Accounts; Variations.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the traditional procurement methods for construction projects.
Summarise the key legal responsibilities of the parties to a construction contract.

Critically analyse from a legal perspective the express nature of contract, time, payment and variations contractual clauses to be found in the AS 4000 standard form general conditions of construction contracts and relate to the contract administration procedures used on construction projects.
Critically review and advise on construction contract administration case scenarios in light of express contract clauses, relevant legislation and the common law.
incompatibilities: must not have completed BUIL3024 UO Contract Administration at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed BUIL3010 Contract Administration at the University of South Australia

title: Statistical Machine Learning
syllabus_overview: This course aims to equip learners with the knowledge and skills to use the modern predictive machine learning models, including kernel methods, Bayesian machine learning and deep learning. Building upon concepts of predictive modelling introduced earlier, the course delves into the foundation mathematics and properties of the methods mentioned above with a focus on how to ensure that these models precisely model the dataset considered. By studying the properties and interpretation of the discussed models, learners will develop critical thinking and problem-solving skills essential for utilizing these models to real-world problems. This course aligns with the program's intent to provide a comprehensive understanding of predictive modelling in modern data science.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the compromises made in machine learning
Describe and interpret the application of deep learning models to real-world datasets
Elucidate the foundation mathematics of deep learning, ensemble models and Bayesian machine learning
Debate the concerns with and ethics of “black-box” modelling when implement policies
prerequisites: Must have completedSTATX200Probability
corequisites: Must be enrolled in MATHX302 Advanced Optimisation

title: Soil Mechanics
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: The aims of the soil mechanics course encompass fostering engineering knowledge and research skills while promoting lifelong learning and complex problem-solving abilities. Through effective communication and teamwork, students will gain proficiency in understanding the origin and composition of soil, phase relationship and soil classification, compaction, effective stresses, seepage and liquefaction, consolidation, shear strength, and loading induced stresses and displacements.
learning_outcomes: Classify different types of soil and determine their engineering properties
Analyse soil compaction and other ground improvement techniques
Explain and calculate the influence of water flow on the engineering behaviour of soils
Evaluate the compressibility of soils and load-induced stress and displacements
Examine and calculate the shear strength of soils
Interpret experimental data and report the results of laboratory experiments to a professional standard
prerequisites: Must have completedENGI1011Engineering Geology and Surveying
corequisites: Must be enrolled inENGM2008Mechanics of Materials and Structures
incompatibilities: Must not have completed CIVENG 2004 Introduction to Geo-engineering at the University of Adelaide OR must not have completed CEME2004 Introduction to Geo-engineering at the University of Adelaide OR must not have completed C&ENVENG2069 Geotechnical Engineering II at the University of Adelaide OR must not have completed CIVE3008 Soil Mechanics at the University of South Australia

assessment_tasks.task_name: Assignment, Assignment, Assignment, Assignment, Assignment, Assignment, Assignment

title: Tourism and Environment
syllabus_overview: Tourism has become one of the largest industries in the world in terms of employment and international trade. On the other hand, public concerns have been growing for the environmental, ecological, and social impacts of tourism, such as the overuse of natural resources, carbon emissions, neoliberalism-driven tourism industry. This course investigates tourism impacts on natural, social, and economic environments at tourism destinations. The course considers the recreational, educational, and economic aspects of tourism associated with protected areas, agricultural landscapes, green open spaces, and cultural assets.
learning_outcomes: Explain the concept of sustainable tourism in using natural resources.
Identify issues associated with social disputes over the use of natural resources for tourism purposes.
Develop and discuss appropriate policy approaches to overcoming tourism-induced environmental problems and to promoting sustainable tourism.
Present and justify the characteristics of nature-based tourism from consumer and producer perspectives.
Convey ideas, using the knowledge gained through class participation, seminar presentation, and essay writing.

title: Development Regulation
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will interpret and relate the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act and Regulations, to building, planning and environmental controls and their application to development and to the practice of building surveying and planning. The Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act and Regulations, Local Government Act, the National Construction Code Volume 1, building approvals and certification, State and Local Government Strategic planning, and planning assessment and the appeals process.
learning_outcomes: Relate the principles of development and control to various projects and localities.
Critically review the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act and Regulations and the related Australian standards.
Relate the Building Code of Australia to projects of all kinds using drawings and other information.
Compose reports on building and planning matters and analyse non-compliance with regulations.
incompatibilities: must not have completed BUIL4030 UO Development Regulation at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed BUIL4028 Development Regulation at the University of South Australia

title: Global Political Economy
syllabus_overview: Neoliberalism is a pivotal concept in contemporary discussions about the global political economy. This course aims to familiarise students with the origins, theories, and applications of neoliberalism globally. It commences by delving into the foundational principles of neoliberal thought, followed by an exploration of the institutional and social changes that have occurred since the neoliberal revolution, alongside alterations in economic structures and the mechanisms of capital accumulation across the world. Throughout the course, students encounter diverse scholarly perspectives on neoliberalism and its different manifestations, culminating in an analysis of its role in global crises and its future trajectories.
learning_outcomes: Articulate the basic contours of neoliberal ideas and practices, and how they have shaped the global political economy.
Identify and analyse different neoliberal trajectories across the world
Think critically about the impact of neoliberalism on states, societies, individuals and the global political economy.
Perform independent research into the history, ideas and practices of neoliberalism, using a diverse range of sources.
Construct persuasive arguments about neoliberalism, and how it relates to global political economy.
Communicate original ideas about neoliberalism with confidence, consideration, and respect.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Multiple Choice Questions, Multiple Choice Questions, Multiple Choice Questions, Multiple Choice Questions

title: Human-Computer Interaction
syllabus_overview: This course aims to provide students with a comprehensive introduction to the foundational research methods and measurement of human-computer interaction (HCI). It covers core concepts, principles, and methodologies, including user-centred design, usability evaluation, and interface prototyping. Students will learn how to apply these concepts to design effective user interfaces, enhance user experiences, and consider the ethical implications of design practices and products.
learning_outcomes: Explain core HCI concepts and human factors in system design and evaluation.
Apply HCI theories and models to analyze and inform system and interface design.
Design and implement interactive prototypes to demonstrate HCI principles.
Evaluate user research methods to select appropriate approaches for studying HCI.
Assess ethical, cultural, and societal issues in HCI
prerequisites: Must have completed COMP1002 Problem Solving and Programming
incompatibilities: Must not have completed UniSA INF1520

title: Circular Economy and Lifecycle Assessment
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: The dominant linear economy (make > use > dispose) wastes resources, is economically inefficient and leads to environmental damage. In a circular economy, the maximum value is extracted from resources in use, then products and materials are recovered and regenerated at the end of each service life. This course will introduce students to the systems thinking required to develop technological solutions and business models that contribute to making our economy more circular. Students will conduct a basic lifecycle assessment to quantify environmental impacts for different product options and will consider case studies of best practice for different circular strategies.
learning_outcomes: Apply established conceptual models and frameworks to explain how materials and energy flows through our economic system
Analyse data from a real-world application to articulate the distinguishing characteristics of different strategies towards a more circular economy
Implement a lifecycle assessment of a product to identify trade-offs between design options, corresponding impacts and sensitivity to modelling assumptions

Use industry standard software to implement and analyse life cycle assessments of increasing sophistication that quantify system wide impacts (e.g. embodied energy, water, land-use and carbon impacts) for design alternatives on a common industry relevant case study

Undertake an open-ended, independent and detailed lifecycle assessment comparing multiple infrastructure options from a realistic design specification. Demonstrate clear interpretation of lifecycle impacts in the context of system boundaries, data suitability and related assumptions.

title: Hydrology and Flood Management
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: To equip students with the skills required to quantify flood risk for design purposes and effectively manage flood events in diverse rural and urban environments. The aim is to prepare students for professional practice. Therefore, students will develop a working knowledge of the national guidelines for flood estimation, Australian Rainfall and Runoff and hands-on experience in using industry-standard software applications for design flood estimation and flood management. The course is offered in a hybrid of project-based and problem-based approaches using design projects from real world case studies
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the key concepts in flood hydrology, flood process, the principles of flood frequency analysis, design rainfall estimation, event-based rainfall-runoff modelling, and the key design considerations of urban stormwater systems.
Apply knowledge and principles of peak flow estimation by using at-site and regional flood frequency analyses to quantify flood magnitudes

Apply knowledge and principles of design flood estimation to use design storm estimation, an event-based rainfall-runoff model, including the principles of model development, calibration, and evaluation approaches to investigate the impact of changes (climate and/or land-use) on the design flood hydrograph

Critically analyse, independently identify and apply the most appropriate flood estimation techniques to generate innovative solutions to complex engineering problems in flood estimation and management of a catchment of interest
Apply the principles of urban stormwater management to design and assess an urban stormwater management system
prerequisites: Must have completed ENGC2000 Introduction to Water Engineering
incompatibilities: Must not have completed CIVE5065 Design of Flood and Drainage Systems at University of South Australia OR must not have completed CIVILENG3004 Hydrology and Flood Management at the University of Adelaide OR must not have completed CIVILENG7304 Hydrology and Flood Management at the University of Adelaide

assessment_tasks.task_name: Interactive Questions, Design Project, Design Project

title: Building Surveying (UniSA)
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will analyse the Australian Standards and National Construction Code requirements for the design and construction of Class 1 and 10 buildings. Students will demonstrate an understanding of building surveying scientific principles used in the design and operation of Class 1 and 10 developments. The (National Construction Code) Building Code of Australia Volume 2 and associated Australian Standards. Design and assessment of residential buildings. Requirements for structural adequacy, specifically timber-framed construction. Fire safety, energy efficiency, health and amenity requirements for residential buildings. Bushfire mitigation measures for design and construction of residential buildings. Deemed-to-satisfy assessment and performance consideration of design and engineering solutions of buildings and structures.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the design and construction of residential buildings in accordance with the National Construction Code and related Australian Standards and explain the concept of the performance based National Construction Code.
Create and use sketch plans, elevations, sections and specifications to communicate construction elements.
incompatibilities: must not have completed CIVE3012 Building Surveying at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed CIVE3015 UO Building Surveying at the University of South Australia

title: Honours Nursing Research Project T/Y Part 4
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to allow students to work with a supervisor to identify a suitable research question, conduct a literature review and prepare a research proposal for submission to the appropriate ethics committee. Students will then continue to work with a supervisor to conduct the research study proposed present their findings in a School of Nursing seminar and in a paper suitable for publication.
prerequisites: Must have completed all of NURS1007 Honours Nursing Research Project T/Y Part 1/NURS1008 Honours Nursing Research Project T/Y Part 2/NURS1009 Honours Nursing Research Project T/Y Part 3
incompatibilities: Must not have completed all of NURS1010 Honours Nursing Research Project T/Y Part 4/NURSING4420D Honours Nursing Research Project T/Y Part 4 at the University of Adelaide

title: Research Skills
syllabus_overview: This course aims to equip students with the knowledge and skills to perform independent research through a systematic approach using the scientific method, covering all areas of research such as literature reviews, methodologies, experimental design, analysis and ethics. Students will delve into research methodologies, ethics and related topics to support them in performing independent research.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate complex information and ideas to propose and design a comprehensive research proposal, incorporating appropriate methodologies and theoretical frameworks relevant to computer science
Analyse quantitative and qualitative data using relevant tools
Communicate complex information and concepts to broad audiences by presenting research and research findings through written reports, presentations, and publications, adhering to academic standards
Apply ethical and cultural frameworks, principles and practices in conducting and reporting research, ensuring integrity and compliance with professional standards
Describe current research-based knowledge and technical and/or creative skills in computer science
Apply research methods, techniques and tools applicable to computer science research
prerequisites: Must have completed 96 units of study

title: Sport Psychology
syllabus_overview: To extend knowledge of health, exercise and sport psychology principles to determine the social, psychological and environmental factors that influence exercise and health behaviours, sport participation and human performance, and apply appropriate best-practice behavioural strategies and theories to advance individuals and groups in health, exercise, and sport settings.
learning_outcomes: Explain psychological, social, and environmental determinants of physical activity, exercise and sport participation, and health behaviours.
Explain the relationships between physical activity, sport and exercise, and psychological wellbeing.
Apply behaviour change theories, techniques, and motivational communication strategies to support exercise participation and health behaviours.
Design evidence-informed behaviour change interventions to promote physical activity, exercise, and health behaviour adherence.
prerequisites: Must have completed HUMV1001 Motor Development and Ageing OR must have completed PSYC1001 Understanding Individual Behaviour and Cognition AND must have completedPSYC1003Health and Developmental Psychology
incompatibilities: Must not have completed HLTH3005 Health, Exercise and Sport Psychology

title: Scalable Software Systems Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course will equip students with practical skills and knowledge to build scalable, reliable and robust software systems. Students will learn about scalable architectures, database scaling, architecture design patterns and load testing methods.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate different architectures for scalability, considering their strengths and weaknesses in meeting varying workload demands
Analyse design patterns and optimisation techniques for building large software systems that can scale effectively
Apply database scaling, including sharding, replication, and partitioning to real world scenarios
Select appropriate caching strategies based on workload characteristics and their role in improving scalability
Evaluate techniques for load testing large-scale systems
Apply approaches for building fault-tolerant systems, including redundancy, error handling, and graceful degradation
prerequisites: Must have completed all of COMP3011 Cloud and Concurrent Programming/INFO4000 System Architecture

title: Advanced Reinforced Concrete Design
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: Drawing on skills developed in Reinforced Concrete Design, this course equips students with advanced knowledge of reinforced concrete design including the design of more complex members, design using alternative materials and design using alternative analysis approaches and international design standards.
learning_outcomes: Interpret the material properties performance of fibre reinforced polymer bars and fibre reinforced concrete.
Analyse and design simple and complex members including those constructed from traditional reinforced concrete and those with fibre reinforcement.
Apply the principles of confinement, strut and tie and moment redistribution to the design of elements.
prerequisites: Must have completedENGCX302Reinforced Concrete Design
incompatibilities: Must not have completed CEME4001 Advanced Reinforced Concrete Design at the University of Adelaide

assessment_tasks.task_name: Problem Solving Task, Problem Solving Task, Problem Solving Task

title: Professional Engineering Practice
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: This course introduces learners to the engineering profession with the goal of fostering vital personal and professional skills for sustainable engineering practice. Learners will develop their identity as modern engineers, contributing collaboratively to sustainable and equitable communities. Emphasising the interdisciplinary nature of engineering, themes include intercultural competence and collaboration with First Nations peoples, professional conduct and skills, effective communication, the engineering method from problem formulation through the complete life cycle, ideation and critical assessment of solutions (including critical evaluation of sustainability and socio-economic aspects), alongside basic project management strategies and processes. These themes are explored through team and project-based learning activities.
learning_outcomes: Describe the role and responsibilities of the professional engineer in modern society, identify key attributes of professional engineers, and develop a professional development plan based on an evaluation of personal strengths and areas for improvement incorporating reflective skills to support ongoing personal and professional growth.

Demonstrate an awareness of engineering as a socio-technical profession including the sustainable, environmental, safety, economic, ethical and diverse social, cultural and global contexts in which it is practiced and critically evaluate proposed engineering solutions using these perspectives.
Explain the engineering method from problem formulation through the complete life-cycle, and apply the engineering method to generate and assess ideas and solution alternatives.

Integrate cultural awareness of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander ways of knowing into engineering practice, developing an understanding of inclusive collaboration and respectful engagement with First Nations communities.
Practice professional conduct, inclusive teamwork skills and apply basic project management principles to engineering problems.

Locates and appropriately references reliable and relevant sources of information and demonstrates written, oral and graphical communication skills appropriate for academic and professional engineering contexts.
incompatibilities: Must not have completed ENGG 1003 AND must not have completed ENG 1001

title: UO Development Regulation
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: The aim of this course is to interpret and relate the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act and Regulations, to building, planning and environmental controls and their application to development and to the practice of building surveying and planning. The Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act and Regulations, Local Government Act, the National Construction Code Volume 1, building approvals and certification, State and Local Government Strategic planning, and planning assessment and the appeals process.
learning_outcomes: Relate the principles of development and control to various projects and localities.
Critically review the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act and Regulations and the related Australian standards.
Relate the Building Code of Australia to projects of all kinds using drawings and other information.
Compose reports on building and planning matters and analyse non-compliance with regulations.
incompatibilities: must not have completed BUIL4030 UO Development Regulation at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed BUIL4028 Development Regulation at the University of South Australia

title: Numerical Modelling of Solids and Structures
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the use of advanced numerical methods in the analysis of structures involving common construction materials. Treatment of this topic is intended to focus on application while providing the key underlying theoretical basis of the methods employed.
learning_outcomes: Apply the underlaying techniques of the matrix method to analyse 1D, 2D and 3D truss structures by solving small size numerical examples of trusses in the form of hand calculations.

Apply the underlaying techniques of the matrix method to analyse beams, 2D frame, grillage frame, and 3D frame structures by solving small size numerical examples of frames in the form of hand calculations.

Apply the underlaying techniques of the finite element method to analyse different type of structures idealised as plane stress, plane strain, axisymmetric, and 3D solid problems by employing them in the computer-based project.
Apply the underlaying techniques of the finite element method to analyse plate and shell of structures by employing them in the computer-based project.

Analyse big size real life complex structures of all types mentioned above by applying a commercially available computer software and in-house developed computer codes after undertaking necessary modifications/extensions of the codes to incorporate new capabilities.
prerequisites: Must have completedENGM2008Mechanics of Materials and Structures AND must have completedCOMP1006Engineering Programming

title: Ethical and Legal Challenges in Technology
syllabus_overview: This course aims to equip leaners with knowledge and awareness of a wide range of ethical and legal challenges related to technology focusing on information technology, and to enable them to identify potential issues in real world cases and recommend resolutions. A wide range of issues will be discussed including privacy, data protection, surveillance and monitoring, cybersecurity and cybercrime, intellectual property rights, and other ethical concerns. Learners will develop understanding of such ethical and legal challenges and become capable of identifying and explaining potential issues and recommending prospective resolutions.
learning_outcomes: Explain the ethical and legal theories, frameworks and issues in technology development, deployment, and use across various domains.
Evaluate the ethical and legal challenges in the context of contemporary information technology systems and practice.
Identify and analyse ethical and legal challenges from the use of information technology within organisational contexts.
Recommend strategies, policies or resolutions for ethical and legal challenges in information technology.
Reflect on the human, cultural and societal factors that shape ethical and legal responsibilities in information technology development and use.
incompatibilities: Must not have completed COMPSCI7212 Human and Ethical Factors in Computer Science at the University of Adelaide

title: Structural Mechanics
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to advanced techniques of structural mechanics, which are essential for analysing complex statically indeterminate structures ranging from beams, trusses and frames. In addition to the force-based method such as unit load method, the course introduces the displacement-based method such as slope deflection method that will be the initial foundation of a computer-based analysis technique. The course also covers special topics such as analysis of arches and cables, influence line diagram of bridge girders due to moving wheel loads, and plastic methods of analysis for estimating collapse loads of beams and frames.
learning_outcomes: Apply force-based methods utilising energy principles to analyse statically determinate and indeterminate beams, trusses and frames.
Apply the concepts of a displacement-based method to evaluate deflections of beams and frames
Produce influence line diagrams for bridge girders due to moving loads
Apply theories of the integration method to calculate the deflection of statically determinate beams
Undertake a computer-based project to analyse statically determinate and indeterminate beams, trusses and frames using a commercially available computer software used in Australian industry.
prerequisites: Must have completed all of ENGM1000 Introduction to Engineering Mechanics/ENGM2008 Mechanics of Materials and Structures
incompatibilities: Must not have completed CIVE3011 Structural Analysis at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed CEME2002 Structural Mechanics at the University of Adelaide

title: Occupational Therapy Field Practice 401
syllabus_overview: The aim of this course is to enable students to consolidate and apply in a practice environment the knowledge, skills and behaviours developed in the academic program. Orientation workshop including expectations and assessment; therapist; application of knowledge and skills gained in the academic program to the practice setting; use of self-directed online learning to explore and extend knowledge and issues that arise from the placement experience; debrief session upon completion of placement.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge and skills to the development and provision of occupational therapy services, to a level of competence consistent with an entry level occupational therapist
Undertake primary responsibility, under supervision, for planning, implementing monitoring, evaluating and reporting occupational therapy programs
Demonstrate respectful practice and advanced level interpersonal skills when communicating and liaising with the client, family, health professionals and other key stakeholders
Demonstrate an ability to function effectively as a member of a health care team
Demonstrate and apply an in-depth knowledge of occupational therapy theory, process and strategies.
Demonstrate safe professional and ethical behaviour consistent with the requirements of an entry level occupational therapist in the practice setting
Comply with policies and procedures relevant to the field practice setting
incompatibilities: Must not have completed all of OCCU4001 Occupational Therapy Field Practice 401/REHB4028 Occupational Therapy Field Practice 401 at the University of South Australia

assessment_tasks.task_name: Placement or Workplace-based Assessment, Learning Journal

title: Clinical Trials: Design and Analysis
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the principles underlying the ethical design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, and reporting of randomised controlled trials in health and medical research. Using real trial examples, it examines how experimental studies with humans generate evidence used in clinical and public-health decision making, including when and why randomised trials may be limited or inappropriate. Core features of well-designed trials, including randomisation, appropriate comparison groups, transparent reporting guided by CONSORT principles, and sound statistical analysis, are examined. Through online content, workshops, and practicals using Stata, students develop practical skills to analyse trial data and critically evaluate evidence to support thoughtful, evidence-based decision making.
learning_outcomes: Explain the fundamental principles underpinning randomised controlled trials, and why these are essential for causal inference.
Apply core design principles to define appropriate populations, interventions, comparators, outcomes, hypotheses, and analysis principles for randomised controlled trials.
Analyse and interpret data from randomised controlled trials using appropriate statistical methods and statistical software (Stata).
Critically evaluate trials against the CONSORT guidance.

Judge the generalisability and real-world relevance of trial evidence, including distinctions between efficacy and effectiveness and implications for policy, practice, and public-health decision-making.
Interpret evidence from experimental studies, articulating design rationale, statistical reasoning, and conclusions appropriate for scientific and public-health audiences.
prerequisites: must have completed 1 of PUBH2007 Essentials of Biostatistics/STAT1000 Data Skills for Scientists

title: Computer Vision and Multimodal Machine Learning
syllabus_overview: This course aims to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of computer vision and multimodal machine learning techniques. Students will explore the theoretical foundations and practical applications of these technologies, gaining skills in designing, implementing, and evaluating models that integrate visual and multimodal data. The course will prepare students for advanced research or professional roles in fields that require sophisticated image and data analysis capabilities.
learning_outcomes: Explain the fundamental concepts and applications of computer vision and multimodal machine learning.
Preprocess images and extract meaningful features for analysis.
Design, implement, and train convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image classification and object detection tasks.
Integrate and analyse multimodal data combining different types of data (e.g., text, image, and audio
Apply advanced techniques such as generative models, transfer learning, and reinforcement learning to improve model performance.
Develop and execute a comprehensive capstone project that demonstrates the ability to solve a complex problem using computer vision and multimodal machine learning techniques.
prerequisites: Must have completed all of COMP5004 Programming for Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning/STAT5020 Statistical Foundations for Data Science and Artificial Intelligence

title: Advanced Concepts in Media and Communication
school: School of Comm, Media and Jour
syllabus_overview: This course aims to develop in students an advanced understanding of some of the most important concepts, theories and ideas in media and communication studies. Building on the first-year course, Key Concepts in Media and Communication, concepts and theories will be related to existing cultural, social and political systems, patterns, issues and debates. Students will develop the tools to apply concepts and theories to some of the most pressing issues, tensions and questions facing the field of media and communication today.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an advanced and detailed understanding of key media and communication theories and concepts
Apply advanced concepts and theories to current problems, issues and debates related to the role of media and communication in social, cultural and political life
Use an advanced understanding of concepts and theories to develop an informed argument for the role of media and communication in society today
Use theory and concepts to critically reflect on media and communication policies, values, professional norms, and other related issues across a range of sectors
prerequisites: must have completed MDIA1018 Key Concepts in Media and Communication

title: UO System Design Practice
syllabus_overview: The aim of this course is to derive a design from a set of system requirements. Participate in design studio to design a viable product; contribute to teams to bring output to stakeholders; and understand the employment market.
learning_outcomes: Develop a high level system design based on a set of requirements.
Apply composition, decomposition and abstraction techniques to generate a component structure for design.
Verify design against requirements to confirm validity of design.
Develop employability skills.
prerequisites: Must have completed INFO2026 UO System Design and Realisation
incompatibilities: Must not have completed INFS2047 UO System Design Practice at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed COMPSCI1106 Introduction to Software Engineering at the University of Adelaide

title: Soil and Groundwater Remediation
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: The course explores the key engineering principles of soil and groundwater remediation. It covers methods for modelling groundwater flows and contaminant transport, estimation of human and ecosystem health risks, and design / implementation of remediation options for contaminated sites. The topics are illustrated using case studies from historical and contemporary practices.
learning_outcomes: Explain the main scientific and engineering principles of soil and groundwater contamination and remediation
Identify human and environmental health issues in relation to redevelopment of contaminated sites
Model groundwater flows using standard equations and techniques
Interpret and summarise principles of assessment of a contaminated site
Apply design principles to recommend feasible remedies for contaminated sites
prerequisites: Must have completed ENGVX200 Environmental Modelling and Management
incompatibilities: Must not have completed ENV ENG 4008 Remediation of Soil & Groundwater Pollution OR must not have completed ENV ENV 7408 Remediation of Soil & Groundwater Pollution

assessment_tasks.task_name: Short Response Questions, Problem Solving Task, Short Response Questions, Short Response Questions

title: Traffic and Transport Modelling
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: This course aims to provide students with an understanding, skills, and knowledge of traffic flow theory, traffic control devices, and travel demand forecast models. It will also emphasise the importance of effectively communicating technical materials to high-level decision-makers through industry-standard software.
learning_outcomes: Explain traffic flow theory, microscopic simulation models and traffic signal design principles.
Apply simulation and analytical tools to evaluate road network performance using industry-standard software.
Analyse and assess traffic signal performance using industry-standard software.
Apply statistical and mathematical techniques for each stage of the travel demand forecasting process.
Develop a four-stage travel demand forecast model and calibrate it using real or hypothetical data with industry-standard software.
Communicate technical information clearly through written reports.
incompatibilities: Must not have completed CIVE4039 Traffic Engineering at the University of South Australia

assessment_tasks.task_name: Short Response Questions, Short Response Questions, Short Response Questions

title: Leadership and Management in Nursing and Midwifery
syllabus_overview: In this course students will be equipped with the knowledge and skills to develop leadership and/or management roles in nursing, midwifery and health services. Theories of leadership and management and their application to nursing, midwifery and health services; emotional intelligence; building resilience; creating influence; change management (leading and building multi disciplinary teams); organisational development, nursing and multi-disciplinary staff development, mentoring staff; performance management; managing staff; resource management.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse leadership styles and management processes in nursing and midwifery context.
Apply theories and principles of leadership to progress nursing and midwifery models of care.
Differentiate between leadership and management.
Explain how leadership development and leadership skills are used to build high performing multi-disciplinary teams.
Discuss the key challenges for leadership in contemporary health systems.
Design an approach to leadership that could result in successful transformation in the workplace.
incompatibilities: must not have completed NURS5150 Leadership and Management in Nursing and Midwifery at the University of South Australia

title: Prestressed Concrete Design
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: This course equips students with skills to design prestressed concrete including the design of beams and slabs for flexure and shear and the design and detailing of anchorages.
learning_outcomes: Describe the principles of prestressed concrete design, including the components, method of action, common applications and design considerations
Analyse and design flexural members subjected to bending and shear
Design and detail anchorage zones to resist bursting and allow for stress transfer and development
Demonstrate application of AS3600 to the design of prestressed concrete elements at the serviceability and ultimate limit state
prerequisites: Must have completedENGCX302Reinforced Concrete Design
incompatibilities: Must not have completed CIVE5079 Advanced Concrete Structures at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed CIVILENG4001 Advanced Reinforced Concrete Design at the University of Adelaide

assessment_tasks.task_name: Problem Solving Task, Problem Solving Task

title: Water Resources Planning and Management
school: School of Civil Eng & Cons Mgt
syllabus_overview: The aim of this course is to prepare students for professional practice in water resources management. The design, planning and management of water resource systems (either regional or local scale) requires excellent knowledge of hydrology and climate science, water flows, statistics and risk estimation, and a diversity of modelling tools. This course will develop the fundamental understanding as well as the engineering design tools and planning principles to design systems needed to meet the demands of an increasing population and changing climate over the 21st century. The, students will also be given opportunity to get hands-on experience in using industry-standard software applications. The course is offered in a mixed-mode approach encompassing project-based, problem-based and research and investigation approaches.
learning_outcomes: Define, comprehend and apply key concepts/methods, the sustainability framework, supply-demand management, key principles of water sensitive urban design (WSUD) for water harvesting and drought risk assessment for water resource systems design and management
Define and comprehend the principles of stochastic climate models, and rainfall-runoff models for streamflow estimation under current and future climates

Apply industry-standard modelling package(s) to undertake the design of a real-world water resource systems using principles of drought risk assessment and stochastic climate modelling to undertake reservoir sizing, identifying operating rules to meet current and future demands by evaluating/optimising for multiple future scenarios

Comprehend and analyse various aspects of water demands and demand management methods, including water sensitive urban design (WSUD) for urban water demand management, and address complex issues related to water demand and environmental flow management in water resources systems
Understand and apply multi-criteria decision analysis and economic evaluation of a real-world industry-oriented project relating to water resources management.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Problem Solving Task, Design Project, Oral Defence
Report, Problem Solving Task, Design Project

title: Interactive Systems Design
syllabus_overview: This course equips learners with the human and technical design skills to create usable interactive systems. Modern interactive systems necessitates a tight coupling between the system feedback (the gulf of evaluation) and the interaction with underlying data, algorithms, and systems (the gulf of execution). Students will practice human centred design processes, usability factors, rapid prototyping, and techniques for reflecting on a design throughout the development process. Students will learn technical skills in architecture design of interactive systems, design patterns, and the use of open-source frameworks to create interactive systems. This course aligns with the program’s aim of designing and developing innovative solutions that demonstrate a high usability.
learning_outcomes: Discuss human centred design methodologies and associated principles for creating interactive systems.
Design the user interface of an interactive system that meet the needs of end-users.
